activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold outside.
story:
Wyatt was at the grocery store with Dad. The freezer door was open. Cold air rushed out at him. Brrr! Wyatt jumped back.

"I want to try," Wyatt said. He put his arms in his coat. He pushed one side into the other side. He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It went wrong at the bottom. He tried again. This time it zipped all the way!

Wyatt stood by the freezer. The cold air bounced off him now. His coat kept his body warm. He smiled a big smile.

"Look, Dad! I did it all by myself," Wyatt said.

"Big news," said Dad. "Now let's go find the bread."

Wyatt zipped his coat again, just to hear the sound. Ziiiip!

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: You can show how old you are by holding up that many fingers.
story:
Miles ran to the picnic table. It was his birthday at the park. Mom had set out cups and a big cake. His friends were coming soon.

A girl named Nia came over. She had never met Miles before. "How old are you?" she asked.

Miles held up his hand. He lifted three fingers. Then he counted them in his head. One, two, three. That was not right. He was one more than three. He put up a fourth finger too.

"Four!" said Nia. "I am four too." She held up four fingers of her own. Their hands looked the same. Miles laughed. So did Nia.

"Can I have cake now?" Miles begged. Dad smiled. "First we light the candles," he said. Dad used a little match. He lit four candles, one for each year. Miles watched from far back, being safe. The candles glowed warm and small.

Everyone sang the song. Then Mom brought Miles a glass of cold juice. He took a big sip. It was sweet and icy. Nia sat right next to him on the bench.

Blow, blow, blow! Miles puffed out all four candles. His friends clapped loud. Nia gave him a high five with her whole little hand.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer and basketball, the referee blows a whistle to stop play.
story:
Maeve sat on the grass with Dad. The soccer game was on the big field. Lots of people ran after the ball. The crowd clapped and cheered.

Maeve wanted to see the ball go in the net. She stood up tall on her tiptoes. The players ran fast. Then a loud sound came. Toot! Toot! A man blew a whistle. All the players stopped running. They stood still on the field.

Maeve looked up at Dad. "Why did they stop?" she asked. "The referee blew his whistle," Dad said. "The whistle stops the game." Maeve watched the man with the whistle. He held up his hand. Then he blew the whistle again. The players began to run once more.

Maeve clapped her hands. Her tummy felt warm and happy. She skipped in a little circle on the grass. Later, the ball flew high and went in the net. Toot! Toot! The game stopped again. Maeve grinned and said, "The whistle did that."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A number word always means the same amount: 'three' always means three things.
story:
Madelyn went to the library with Grandma. It was a sunny morning. Madelyn wanted a book about ducks.

The duck books were on a high shelf. Madelyn could not reach them. "I will help," said Grandma. "First, find them." Madelyn looked and looked. The duck book seemed to hide behind big books.

Grandma sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Madelyn sang too. Then she saw it. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" she sang. On the word "ten," her finger touched the duck book. It was the tenth book on the shelf.

Grandma took it down. "Can I have three books?" Madelyn asked. "Yes, three," said Grandma. Madelyn picked one duck book, one dog book, and one bear book. "Is that three?" she asked. Grandma nodded. "One, two, three," said Grandma. "Three means three books. Big ones and small ones too."

Madelyn counted her books all by herself. One, two, three. Then she counted the steps to the big chair. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. She was not alone. Grandma sat right beside her.

Madelyn hugged her three books. "Ten steps to the door," she said. Grandma laughed. "Let's count them together." They counted one, two, three, all the way to ten. "We made it," said Grandma. Madelyn held her hand tight.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a clear, sunny day, the sky looks blue.
story:
Charlotte went to the store with Mama. She held Mama's hand. The store had crayons in big rows. Charlotte wanted crayons to draw pizza, and the sun, and the sky.

She picked a red crayon for the pizza. Then she picked a yellow crayon for the sun. Then she picked a gray crayon for the sky. "All done," she said.

Mama walked her to the window. "Look up," said Mama. Charlotte looked up. The day was sunny and clear. The sky was not gray. The sky was blue, all over, way up high. Charlotte put the gray crayon back. She took a blue one instead. Then she found a green crayon too, for the grass by her house.

At home, Charlotte tried to draw. She drew red pizza with yellow sun on top. She drew the blue sky over the green grass. Mama pointed at the sky in the picture. "Just like outside," said Mama. Charlotte smiled and held her picture up to the window.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: We wash our hands before we eat.
story:
Michael ran to the table. Grandma had put out warm bread. It smelled so good. He reached out his hand.

Then he stopped. He looked at his fingers. They had dirt on them. He had been helping plant flowers in the yard.

"First I wash," Michael said. He walked to the sink. Grandma smiled and followed him.

He pushed the soap pump. White soap came out. It felt smooth and slippery. He rubbed his hands together. Bubbles grew and grew.

"We wash our hands before we eat," Grandma said. She helped him count. "One, two, three." They counted all the way to twenty.

The water rinsed the bubbles away. His hands were clean now. He dried them on the soft towel.

Michael sat down and took a big bite of bread. Later, after the toilet, he ran to the sink again. He pumped the soap himself.

"Twenty seconds," he said, counting out loud.

Grandma clapped her hands.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: When someone says 'thank you', people often answer 'you're welcome.'
story:
Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a small bag of crackers. Her friend Ben sat next to her. Ben looked at the crackers. "Crackers, please?" said Ben. Sadie held out the bag. Ben took one cracker. He smiled big.

"Thank you," said Ben. Sadie did not know what to say back. She sat quiet. Then she heard her mama at the window. Mama gave the ticket man some money. "Thank you," said the ticket man. "You're welcome," said Mama. Sadie heard it. She tried it in her head. You're welcome. You're welcome.

"Thank you," said Ben again. "You're welcome," said Sadie. Ben laughed. Mama smiled in the mirror. Sadie gave Ben one more cracker. Then the car went over a bump. Sadie's cracker fell on the floor. "Oh no. Can you help, please?" she said. Mama reached back and got it. "You're welcome," said Mama. Sadie ate her cracker. It was cool how that worked.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Two groups have the same number when each object in one group can be matched with one object in the other.
story:
It was snack time at school. Ruby's teacher, Miss Amy, held up a big bag of cups.

"Ruby, can you help?" asked Miss Amy. "Put one cup at each chair."

Ruby looked at the long table. She counted the chairs. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." Eight chairs.

Then Ruby counted the cups in the bag. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." Eight cups. She put one cup at each chair. She put one cup down. She went to the next chair. She put one cup down. Every chair got one cup. The last chair got the last cup.

"What if I had more cups?" Ruby asked herself. She lifted a shiny spoon from the tray and tried it at the last chair. But the chair already had a cup. So there was no chair left for the spoon cup. "The cups are just right," said Ruby. "Each chair has one."

Then Sam came over with a string of napkins. He had napkins for only six chairs.

"Do you have more or less than me?" Sam asked.

"You have less," said Ruby. "See? Only six chairs have napkins. Two chairs have no napkins."

Sam got two more napkins. Now every chair had one napkin. Now every chair had one cup.

Miss Amy smiled. "Snack is ready," she said.

Ruby sat down in her chair. Her cup was there, waiting for her. She picked it up and said, "One cup for me."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Taking photos on a trip lets a family remember it after they get home.
story:
Lea packed her little red bag. "We go to the beach today!" she sang. The car ride was long. Lea counted three cows, then she fell asleep.

At the beach, Lea found a shell. "Mama, look!" she said. Mama held up her phone. "Smile for a photo," said Mama. Click. Lea smiled. Click, click. Papa took a photo of the big waves. Lea took a photo of her toes in the sand. "My toes look funny!" she laughed.

Lea put her shell in the water. It did not float. It sat on the bottom. "Silly shell," said Lea. A wave came and tickled her knees. Click went Mama's phone again.

At home, the beach was gone. Lea felt sad. "I miss the sand," she said. Mama sat down next to her. "Let's look at our trip photos," she said. There was Lea and the shell. There were her funny toes. There was the big wave. Lea giggled and giggled. "Look, Papa, my toes!" she said. Papa laughed too. "That beach was different from our house," he said. Lea pointed at the last photo. "Again," she said. "Again and again."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together.
story:
Athena went to Miss Kim's music room. There was a big drum in the corner. Athena wanted to play it with her friend Tom.

Tom had sticks. Athena had sticks too. They began to tap. Tom tapped fast, fast, fast. Athena tapped slow. The sounds crashed like a stormy sea. It did not sound good.

"Why is it so messy?" Athena asked.

Miss Kim clapped her hands. Tap, tap, tap. She clapped slow and steady. Tom copied her. Athena copied her. Then they tapped the drum together. Tap, tap, tap. It sounded like one big drum!

"Now it sounds happy," said Athena.

They played a song. Miss Kim drew a picture of two drummers holding hands. She hung it on the wall.

Athena looked up at the picture. "Thank you, Miss Kim," she said.

Miss Kim smiled. "Play it again," she said.

Athena lifted her sticks. Tap, tap, tap.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A vegetable plant that does not get enough water droops.
story:
Nolan ran to the community garden with his small watering can. He had planted lettuce seeds with Grandma last week. Now tiny green leaves peeked out of the dirt. "Hello, little plants!" he said.

The sun was hot that day. Nolan looked at his lettuce. The leaves were drooping. They hung down low, like sleepy heads. "Grandma, why are they sad?" he asked. Grandma filled his can at the pond. "Give them a drink," she said. Nolan poured the smooth, cool water over the leaves. The dirt turned dark and wet.

The next morning, Nolan ran back to the garden. He gasped. The lettuce stood up tall! The leaves were perky and green. "Water made them wake up!" he said. He patted the dirt gently. "I will bring you water every day, little plants." Grandma smiled and gave him a big high five.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cake batter is runny when it goes into the oven and comes out as a cake you can slice.
story:
Theodore held his mama's hand at the farmers' market. "Strawberries!" he shouted. "Can we get some?" Mama laughed. "Yes. Today we bake a cake." Theodore jumped up and down. A cake! A whole cake! They knocked on the farmer's window to pay for the eggs. The farmer smiled and handed them over, one by one.

At home, Theodore helped at the big table. He cracked the eggs into the bowl. He poured in the flour. He stirred and stirred. A tiny taste of strawberry went in his mouth. The rest went in the bowl. Then Theodore looked in the bowl and stopped. The batter was runny. It was thin and wobbly like a puddle.

"Mama, it's broken!" he said. "Cake is big and round. This is just goo." His lip wobbled. "It will never be a cake." Mama carried the bowl to the oven. "In it goes," she said. Theodore stood far back, where it was safe. The oven door closed with a soft thump.

Theodore pressed his nose to the kitchen window. Outside, a cloud looked like a lion with a big fluffy mane. The kitchen began to smell sweet. "Sniff, sniff," said Theodore. "Mmm!" His tummy made a happy little growl. Then the timer went ding!

Mama opened the oven door. She used her big mitts. Out came a real cake! It was tall and golden. It was not runny at all. Mama set it down and cut one slice. The slice stood up on the plate, all by itself. Theodore clapped his hands. "It's a cake now!" he said. "Can we eat the lion-sized piece?"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Snow melts into water when it is brought inside where it is warm.
story:
Lucy woke up and saw snow. "No school today!" said Mom. Lucy put on her red boots and her funny hat with a leaf print on it.

Lucy went to the big sledding hill. She slid down, down, down. Whee! Then she made a snowball. It was round and white. She wanted to keep it. Mom helped her lock the door and they went inside, out of the cold.

Lucy set the snowball in a bowl on the table. "Now it will stay," she said. She ate lunch. She looked again. The snowball was small. She looked later. Where did it go? There was only water in the bowl. Lucy touched it with one finger. Mom smiled. "Want to make a new one outside?" Lucy ran for her boots. "Yes! A big one this time!"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: People often write their name on their artwork so everyone knows who made it.
story:
Maverick sat at the little table. He had red paint, blue paint, and one big brush. He painted a cat. The cat had a long tail. "One tail, two ears, three whiskers," he said. He counted each part as he painted.

His friend Nia sat next to him. She painted a cat too. Her cat also had a long tail. The two cats looked almost the same. Then it was time for snack. The teacher said, "Put your papers on the big rack." Maverick put his cat on the rack. Nia put her cat on the rack too.

After snack, Maverick ran back. He saw two cats on the rack. "Which one is mine?" he asked. "I can't tell." Nia looked too. "I can't tell either," she said. The cats were the same size. The tails were the same brown. Both had one, two, three whiskers.

Then Miss Kim, the kind teacher, came over. She held up one paper. At the bottom were small letters. "This says Nia," she said. "Nia wrote her name on her art." Maverick looked at the other paper. No name. No letters. Just his cat. "That one is mine," he said. "It has no name on it." He took his cat and gave Nia hers. Nia smiled. "Thank you," she said.

Miss Kim gave Maverick a crayon. "You can write your name too," she said. Maverick held the crayon. He made an M. He made an A. He wrote every letter, one by one. Then he held up his cat. "Now it says Maverick," he said. "Now everyone knows it is mine."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
fact: Looking at the target while you throw helps you aim.
story:
Brielle ran into the sunny backyard. Dad held up a big red hoop. "Time to play!" he said. "Throw the beanbag in!"

Brielle held her yellow beanbag. She looked at Dad and waved. Then she threw the beanbag. It fell in the grass. Not in the hoop!

Mom rolled a big blue ball to Brielle. Brielle looked up at a bird. The ball bumped her tummy and rolled away. "Oh no!" said Brielle.

"Try again," said Dad. He blew a whistle. Pop! The sound made Brielle giggle.

Brielle picked up the beanbag. This time she looked at the hoop. Only the hoop. She threw the beanbag. In it went! "Yes!" she shouted.

Mom rolled the big ball again. Brielle looked at the ball. Only the ball. She held out both hands. Thump! The ball landed right in her arms.

"One beanbag, one ball, one hoop!" said Brielle. Dad clapped. Mom clapped. The wind blew the leaves around.

Brielle threw the beanbag again, looking at the hoop the whole time. In it went again!

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a sunny day, a sun hat helps shade your face.
story:
Claare stood at the front door. She wanted to play outside. The sun was very bright. "It is sunny today," said Mom.

Claire ran to the yard. The sun shone on her face. She squeezed her eyes shut. It was too bright to see the swing. "Ow," said Claire. She held her hand over her eyes.

Mom came out with a hat. It had a big brim. "Here is your sun hat," said Mom. Claire put it on. The brim made shade over her face. Now she could open her eyes wide. She could see the swing and the whole yard. "I can see now!" said Claire.

Then the wind blew. The wind took Claire's paper boat right off the step. Claire chased her boat to the fence. Dad picked it up for her. "It is windy too," said Claire. She held her boat tight. Dark clouds came. A few drops fell. "Rainy soon," said Dad. "Get your rain boots." Claire stomped inside in her boots, and the rain began to tap on the door.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: If two children want the same toy, a grown-up can help them take turns.
story:
Layla was at school. She saw a red truck on the rug. It had big black wheels. She wanted it fast.

But Tom grabbed the truck too. Layla pulled one end. Tom pulled the other end. The truck could not move.

"Let's ask Miss Jo," said Tom. Miss Jo came over. She held up the truck. "You can take turns," she said. "Tom first. Layla, you can have the next turn."

Layla sat on the rug. She waited. She watched Tom push the truck. It went far, far across the floor. Then Tom brought it back.

"Your turn now," said Tom. Layla took the truck. She pushed it fast. It rolled under the little table. Tom laughed and clapped.

"Here," said Layla. She held out the truck. "Your turn again."

Tom smiled big. "This is fun," he said. Then he pushed the truck past the blocks.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Small toys can roll or slide under furniture like couches and beds.
story:
Ibrahim went to the park on a cold winter day. He carried his little red marble in his pocket. At the park he set it on the wooden bench. Then the wind blew. The marble rolled and dropped off the bench.

Ibrahim looked on the ground. He looked by the tree. No marble. "I will try one more place," he said. He got down on his knees. He peeked under the bench. There it was! The marble had rolled under the bench and sat in the cool brown leaves. Yesterday his marble had slid under the couch at home. He had found it way in the back. This morning it rolled under his bed, and he found it there too. Small toys always seemed to roll or slide under things and hide.

A little girl walked up with her mother. "My ball went under the bench," she said. "I can't reach it." Ibrahim stood up and pointed. "Look under there," he said. The girl bent down and peeked. Her yellow ball was resting in the leaves next to a shiny bottle cap. She reached in and pulled out her ball. "A treasure!" she said, holding up the bottle cap too. Ibrahim held his warm marble in his hand and smiled. The wind blew again, and the leaves went shhh, shhh across the grass.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: Many drawing apps let you pick a colour by tapping it.
story:
Leah sat on the living room rug. She wanted to draw a big red sun. Mom handed her the tablet.

"First, you press the round button," said Mom. Leah pressed it with one finger. The screen lit up. Then Leah tapped the little picture with the crayons. The drawing app opened.

Leah touched the blue spot first. Her finger made a blue line. "I want red," she said. "Where is red?" She looked at all the little circles. She found a red one and tapped it. Her next line came out red. "Red!" she laughed. She drew a big round sun with red rays. Then she drew green grass at the bottom.

"Now what do I do?" Leah asked.

"You hold the button again, and the screen goes to sleep," said Mom. Leah held the button. The screen went dark. She put the tablet on the shelf, right where it lives.

"Can I draw again after my nap in bed?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "The sun will wait for you."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Covering different holes on a recorder makes different notes.
story:
Theo went to the community center with his mama. There was a music room with little chairs. On a table lay some recorders.

A girl named Mei had a yellow duck on her shirt. It was her favorite shirt. Mei picked up a recorder and blew. Squeak! The recorder made a loud squeaky sound. Mei frowned.

Theo picked up a recorder too. He put his fingers on the holes. He blew. A nice note came out. Theo lifted one finger off a hole. He blew again. A different note came out! He put his finger back down. The first note came back.

Theo tapped Mei's finger. "Your finger is not on the hole," he said. Mei looked down. She moved her finger. She covered the hole all the way. She blew. A nice note came out! No squeak.

Mei laughed. Theo laughed. They took turns. Theo covered one hole, then another. Each hole made a different note. The teacher played along on her big drum.

Theo blew a long note, and Mei blew one too.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, lion dancers move to the beat of loud drums.
story:
Isabelle went to the cultural center with Mama and Grandpa. It was a rainy day, so the party was all inside. There was a big red and gold lion waiting by the door. Isabelle held Mama's hand.

Boom! Boom! Boom! The drums were so loud. Isabelle jumped and covered her ears. "Too loud," she said. Grandpa knelt down beside her. "It is okay," he said. "Stay with me." Then Isabelle looked at the lion. The lion moved. The drums went boom, and the lion jumped. The drums went boom again, and the lion shook his head.

"Is the lion dancing to the drums?" Isabelle asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "Watch him go." The drums beat faster. The lion hopped and spun. Isabelle let go of her ears. She clapped her hands. Boom, clap, boom, clap! The lion blinked his big eyes at her. "He looked at me!" said Isabelle. Grandpa laughed and held her close. On the way home, Mama said Isabelle would get a warm bath before bed. Isabelle clapped one more time, soft and small.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: A kitchen timer beeps or rings to tell the cook it is time to check the food.
story:
David put muffin mix in a big bowl. His teacher, Miss Anne, helped him stir. David poured the sweet batter into cups. Miss Anne put the pan in the oven. She set a little timer on the table.

Then David's family came to visit. Mama and Papa played a game with David. It was a fox game with a picture of a red fox. David rolled the dice and moved his fox. He laughed a lot.

Then the timer rang. Beep, beep, beep. "The muffins!" said Miss Anne. She took the pan out with big mitts. David got to read the word "muffin" on the box. The muffins were warm and sweet. David gave one to Mama and one to Papa. "Yum," said Papa, and he took a big bite.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: It is okay for a big brother or sister to feel left out when a new baby arrives.
story:
Florence sat in the car. They were going to the hospital. A new baby was coming today.

At the hospital, everyone looked at the baby. They held the baby. They talked to the baby. Nobody looked at Florence. She felt small, like a little mouse.

"I miss you, Mom," Florence said in the car. "Just you and me."

Mom held her hand. "That is okay," Mom said. "Big sisters can feel that way. I still love you."

Florence drew a picture at home. She drew the baby. She drew Mom. She drew herself, right beside them.

Mom put it on the fridge. "The baby is here," Florence said. "And I am here too."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Stopping before the cup is full to the top makes it easier to carry without spilling.
story:
Ali ran into the big kitchen. Snow was falling past the window. "Toast time!" he said.

Miss Jo gave Ali warm bread. A grown-up had cut it for him. Ali took his little knife. It was safe and soft. He spread the butter. The butter made the bread shiny. "Look, Mom! I did it!"

Next came the milk. Ali held the cup under the jug. He poured and poured. The milk went all the way to the top. Ali picked up the cup. He took one step. The milk sloshed. Milk spilled onto the floor.

Miss Jo mopped it up. "Try again," she said. Ali poured the milk again. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. He picked it up. He walked slowly. Not one drop fell out!

"I did it! No spill!" Ali blew on his milk like it was hot cocoa. "You are so cute," said Mom. Ali drank it all up.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: If you hold a book upside down, the words and pictures look upside down too.
story:
Eva went to the library with Dad. She saw a red book on a little table. "I want that one," she said. Dad said, "You can grab it."

Eva grabbed the red book. She held it upside down. The bear on the page stood on his head. The words stood on their heads too. Eva laughed. "Silly bear!"

The librarian walked by. "Oh my," she said. "That bear looks funny." Eva turned the book around. Now the bear stood on his feet. The words stood up too.

Eva opened the front cover. The first page said "bear". Dad pointed at the word. "B says bear," he said. Eva turned one page, then the last page. The story was all done. "Again!" said Eva. Dad smiled. "From the front," he said. Eva flipped the book upside down one more time, and the bear stood on his head again. "Silly bear!" she said.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: In pretend play, a cardboard box can become a car, a boat or a house.
story:
Leah found a big cardboard box at school. She wanted it to be a car. "Beep beep!" she said.

Her friend Tom ran over. He grabbed the box too. "It's a boat!" he said. Tom's face looked sad and hard.

"Wait," said Leah. "You go first." Tom sat in the box. He rowed with a bucket. "The boat needs a baby fish!" he said. Leah hugged her toy bear. She tucked it in a blanket. The baby fish fell asleep.

Then Leah climbed in. "Now it's my turn," she said. "This is my car." Tom made engine sounds for her. The car drove fast. Then it drove home. "We are here!" said Leah. She carried her bear inside the box house. Tom knocked on the wall. "Hello!" he said. "Come in," said Leah. She held the door open for him.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food.
story:
Everly was at Grandma's house. Her new baby brother was there too. He was small and soft. He made tiny sounds.

Everly had a cracker in her hand. She wanted to give it to the baby. She held it out to his mouth. "Here, baby," she said. Grandma came over fast. "Wait, Everly," she said. "The baby cannot eat a cracker yet. A baby drinks milk, not big kid food."

Everly looked at her cracker. Then she looked at the baby. Grandma picked up a little bottle. It was warm from the hot water pot, and now it was cool enough. Grandma held it for the baby. The baby drank and drank. His eyes closed. His little hand held Grandma's finger.

Everly ate her cracker all by herself. Then she patted the baby's blanket. "Next year you can have one," she whispered. At the table, Grandma smiled and put a cookie on Everly's plate. Everly shared her cookie with Grandma, one half each.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups.
story:
Nova's tooth felt wiggly at daycare. She was scared to open her mouth wide. "I don't want it to fall out," she said.

Her teacher Sam sat down next to her. "I felt that way too," Sam said. "My tooth wiggled when I was small. I was nervous. Even grown-ups feel that way. Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups."

Nova looked up. "You were afraid?" she asked. Sam nodded. Nova felt a little braver.

A boy named Max ran by with a big smile. He was so happy. Then he dropped his truck and looked angry. "My truck!" he shouted. Nova picked it up and gave it back. Max smiled again.

"Now I am excited," said Nova. She opened her mouth wide in the mirror. The tooth stayed put, just a little wiggly.

Sam laughed. "It will come out when it is ready," Sam said. Nova wiggled it with her finger and smiled back.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Starting a question with 'May I' is a polite way to ask permission.
story:
Mason wanted to hold the lion puppet. His sister Lily had it. She waved it up and down. The lion gave a big shake of its mane.

Mason reached out. He grabbed the lion's tail. Lily pulled it back. "No," she said. "You didn't ask."

Mason felt like crying. Mama came close. "Say, 'May I have a turn?'" said Mama. Mason took a big breath. "May I have a turn, please?" he asked.

Lily smiled. "Yes! Here you go." She put the lion in his hands. The lion gave Mason a kiss on his nose. "Thank you," said Mason. Then the lion jumped too high and bumped Lily's head. "Sorry," said Mason. He patted her arm.

Mason shook the lion gently. Lily clapped. "What a polite lion," said Mama. Mason hugged the puppet tight. "May I keep him a little more?" he asked. "Yes," said Lily. And the lion danced on Mason's knee.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Things can be sorted into groups, like animals, toys and foods.
story:
Weston ran to the toy corner at daycare. There was a big basket on the floor. His friend Mia tipped it over. Lots of picture cards fell out everywhere.

"Let's put them in piles," said Mia. Weston picked up a card. It had a cow on it. Mia held up a card with a dog. "Dogs and cows are animals," she said. "They go in one pile."

Weston found a card with a banana. It did not go with the cow. He found a card with an apple. Bananas and apples were foods. He made a new pile for foods. Then he found a ball card and a triangle block card. Those were toys. Toys got a pile too.

Soon all the cards were in three neat piles. Teacher Jo smiled. "What nice piles," she said. "Look, animals, foods, and toys." Weston clapped his hands. Then he and Mia picked one card from each pile. A cat, a carrot, and a drum. "The cat eats the carrot," Weston said. Mia laughed. "Then the cat plays the drum."

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'hello' when you meet someone is a friendly way to greet them.
story:
Violet ran to the swings with her dad. A new girl stood by the slide. She hid behind her mom.

The girl's mom waved at Violet. Violet hid behind her dad. Then she peeked out. "Hello," said Violet, in a small voice. The girl peeked out too. "Hello," said the girl. Now they both smiled.

"Swing with me? Please?" said Violet. The girl nodded. They pumped their legs high. "Thank you for asking me," said the girl.

The girl fell in the sand. "Sorry," said Violet, "I zipped too fast." She ran to her dad. "Dad, help, please." Dad helped the girl up and brushed off the sand. The girl laughed. "I am okay. Sand is not itchy."

Then something small surprised them. The girl had a whistle in her pocket. Toot, toot! Violet giggled. "Hello, whistle," said Violet.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A map shows roads and places, so people can find the way somewhere new.
story:
Sienna sat by the train window. She was going on a big family trip. Her friend Bear sat on her lap. "One suitcase, two snacks, three hugs," Mama counted. Papa held a big paper map.

The train stopped at a little station. The family got off. They walked to the car. Papa drove and drove. Then the road looked wrong. "Oh dear," said Papa. "I think we took a wrong turn."

Mama opened the map. Sienna peeked at it. The map had roads, small and thin like noodles. It had towns, little dots. "Look," said Sienna. She put her finger on a dot. "That is our town." Her finger slid along a road. "This road goes to the sea."

Papa smiled. "Let us follow the road on the map." He turned the car around. They drove past a cow. They drove past one windmill, two windmill... no, three windmills!

The air smelled fresh and salty. "The sea!" said Sienna. She rolled down the window a little bit. Her ice cream began to melt in the sun. She licked it fast. "The map found the way," she said. Papa laughed. "It did, little helper." Sienna gave Bear a sticky, sweet hug.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: The author is the person who wrote the words of a book.
story:
Aaron was at Grandma's house. He wanted a story, but Grandma was fixing lunch. "Find a book," she said. "Then we will read it together."

Aaron hurried to the book shelf. He picked his favorite book. It had a bear on the front. He saw little marks all over the pages. "Grandma, what are these marks?" he asked.

"Those are words," said Grandma. "Words tell the story." She opened the book. "We start at the front," she said. "Then we go page by page." Grandma read the words out loud. The bear found a honey pot! Aaron clapped. The words made that happen.

Then Aaron asked, "Who made up the bear story?" Grandma pointed to the cover. "See this name?" she said. "That is the author. The author is the person who wrote the words of the book." Aaron said the name out loud. "The author wrote my bear!"

Every night after that, Aaron looked for the author's name. He found it on his truck book. He found it on his dog book. "The author wrote the words," he said, and smiled at the name.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: The dentist's chair tips back so you lie down while the dentist looks in your mouth.
story:
Willow sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist for the first time. "Will it hurt?" she asked. "No," said Dad. "But I don't know what happens there," said Willow. "We can find out together," said Dad.

At the dentist's office, Willow saw a big chair. She did not want to sit in it. The dentist smiled. "Just sit and try," she said. Willow sat down. Then she pressed nothing at all, and the chair began to move. It slowly tipped back! Willow was lying down now, just like in bed. "It moved!" she said. "It tips back so I lie down!" "Yes," said the dentist. "Now I can look in your mouth." Willow opened her mouth wide. She felt brave and smart.

On the ride home, Willow smiled. "Dad, the chair fell back like a ride at the park!" "It did," said Dad. Willow said, "I want to lift my hand and wave goodbye to the chair." She lifted her hand and waved all the way out the door. "Bye, big chair!"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing blue paint and yellow paint makes green.
story:
Joshua sat at the picnic table at summer camp. He wore his big yellow hat. The sun was high in the sky. He was painting a picture of grass. But Joshua had a problem. He had blue paint and yellow paint. He did not have green paint. Grass is green, and his paper grass looked all wrong in blue.

"I need green," Joshua said. His friend Mia sat down next to him. She sang a little song while she painted. Joshua dipped his brush in the blue paint. Then he dipped it in the yellow paint. He stirred them together on his plate. The paint turned green! Joshua opened his mouth wide. He looked at his brush. It was green, really green.

"Look, Mia!" he said. He painted tall green grass all over his paper. Then he painted a green hill, too. The birds sang up in the trees. Joshua held up his painting so Mia could see it. "Blue and yellow make green," said Joshua, and he painted one more blade of grass.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Toys cannot really feel, but you can pretend they do.
story:
Gabriella went to Mia's house. Mia had a big doll named Rosie. They were playing house. Mia was the mom. Gabriella was the doctor.

Then Mia tripped on the rug. Rosie fell too. She slid under the chair. Mia began to cry.

Mia's dad came in. He picked up Rosie. He looked at her arms and legs. "Rosie cannot really feel hurt," he said. "She is just a toy. But you can give her a pretend hug."

Mia stopped crying. She hugged Rosie tight. Gabriella watched. Then she had an idea. She patted Rosie's head very soft. "All better!" she said. Mia smiled a big smile.

Then they made Rosie swim across the blue blanket. They spotted a spotted sock and made it a fish. Rosie chased the fish. "Swim fast, Rosie!" said Mia.

At dinner time, Gabriella told her mom everything. "Rosie fell down," she said. "But we fixed her with pretend hugs."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: A book in English starts at the front cover, and you turn the pages until you reach the back.
story:
Asher went to the store with Mama. He wanted a book about trucks. One truck, two trucks, three trucks, all on the shelf. "This one," said Asher. It was soft at the corners, just right for his hands.

He sat down to read. But wait. The truck drove backward. The mud was on the first page. The dog barked before he woke up. "Silly book," said Asher. "Your day is all mixed up!" The letters on the back seemed to hide from him. They were upside down too.

Mama smiled. Asher turned the book over. Now he saw the front cover. He opened the front. The truck drove forward. The dog woke up, then he barked. "There you are," said Asher. One page, two pages, three pages, all the way to the back. He hugged the soft book. "We start at the front," said Asher. Then he read it again.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A grandparent can show a child how to make a food their family has made for a long time.
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor wanted to do something big with her. "Can we make your bread?" she asked. "The bread you always bring?" Grandma smiled. "Yes. My mother taught me. Her mother taught her. Our family has made it for a long, long time."

So they began. Eleanor poured flour. It made a tiny white cloud. "Look!" she said. "My hands made the cloud!" Grandma laughed. Eleanor poked the dough. It was soft and squishy in the middle. "Why does it get big?" she wondered. Grandma said, "Wait and see."

They waited. The dough grew puffy. Eleanor skipped around the kitchen while it grew. Then Grandma put the pan in the hot oven. Eleanor watched from her chair.

Out came warm bread. "I helped make this," Eleanor said. She took a big bite. "It tastes just like your bread, Grandma!"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
story:
Cooper ran to the art table. He wore his favorite blue shirt. He wanted to paint a big yellow sun.

The class was noisy with happy painters. Everyone put on an apron. Cooper did not. He was too excited to wait.

He dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He made a circle. Then a drop fell. It landed on his blue shirt. He looked down. A big yellow spot sat on his sleeve.

Cooper's eyes got wide. The teacher came over with a soft smile. She helped him put on an apron. It was red with white dots. It covered his shirt all the way down.

He painted more suns. He painted rays and stars. No more paint got on his clothes. Not one drop.

Then he found a surprise under the paint cups. A tiny glass jar of sparkles! He shook it gently. The sparkles looked like stars on his sun.

"Look at my sun!" said Cooper. The teacher held it up to the window.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Big objects and small objects count the same: three big balls and three tiny beads are both three.
story:
Raphael sat by the big window at the community centre. Miss Dana put out two baskets. One basket held three big balls. The other basket held three tiny beads.

"The balls are more!" said Raphael. "They are so big." He counted the balls. "One, two, three." Then he counted the beads. "One, two, three." He sat very still. "The same? But the beads are so small!"

Miss Dana smiled. "Count them again," she said. He did. Balls: one, two, three. Beads: one, two, three. Big balls and tiny beads both made three.

Then Raphael saw his friend Sam with a broken crayon. Sam looked sad. Raphael tipped the beads into Sam's hand. "Here, you can hold three," he said. "Three beads, three balls. Same!"

Sam laughed and held them up to the window so the sun made them shine.
